nodes_source.source_quote: In this work, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to explore the potential of traffic video data in improving the efficiency of ramp metering.
nodes_source.description: Real-world traffic video data from which vehicle locations are extracted and reformed as position matrices, used as inputs for the deep reinforcement learning method.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: The data used to support the results of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations (x, y) are extracted from raw traffic video frames.

nodes_process.source_quote: traffic state at time step t is represented by a position matrix m₁ ∈ RXxY;
nodes_process.description: Vehicle location points are represented as a position matrix, where Uv is a constant for vehicle positions and signal states are included. Other elements are set to zero.

nodes_process.source_quote: Since one matrix is insufficient to describe vehicle dynamics, we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state s₁: S₁ = {m₁-(N-1),..., m₁}. For computation efficiency, down-sampling is introduced before the matrix stack to reduce the input dimensions and maintain sufficient information about vehicle positions.
nodes_process.description: Consecutive position matrices are stacked to form the state representation. Down-sampling is applied to reduce dimensions and maintain sufficient information about vehicle positions.

nodes_process.source_quote: The reward r₁ after action at is defined by the following: rt = vt + wqt, μ > 0, ω < 0,
nodes_process.description: The reward function is defined as a linear combination of average speed in the merging area (v) and average queue length at the on-ramp (q), with weights mu and omega.

nodes_process.source_quote: The Q-network in Mnih et al. [30] is revised as Figure 7, which consists of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one full connection (FC) layer for each output layer.
nodes_process.description: The Q-network is a deep neural network with three convolutional layers and one fully connected layer, adapted from Mnih et al. [30]. It is extended to two FC layers for multitask learning.

nodes_process.source_quote: The algorithm for training the ramp metering policy is presented in Algorithm 1. The ramp meter takes new action with the e-greedy strategy, meaning that the agent does not always adopt the best action derived from current Q (s, a, w).
nodes_process.description: The DRL agent is trained using Q-learning with Adam optimizer, experience replay, a target network, and an epsilon-greedy strategy. A multitask learning strategy is used to predict speed and queue length simultaneously.

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31].
nodes_process.description: A microscopic traffic simulation environment is set up using SUMO to model the freeway network connecting Qingdao and Huangdao.

nodes_process.source_quote: The PI-ALINEA method fixes the length of the green phase and determines the length of the red phase in the current signal cycle based on the length of the red phase in the previous cycle and the downstream occupancies in the previous and current cycles.
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA ramp metering method is set up as a baseline. It calculates the ramp metering rate based on previous red phase length and downstream occupancies.

nodes_process.source_quote: The Q-network is trained in 10^6 training frames, and each scenario is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments.
nodes_process.description: 20 simulation experiments are conducted for each scenario (no-control, PI-ALINEA, DRL) using the SUMO environment.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 9 presents the Q1 (25%), Q2 (50%), and Q3 (75%) of the travel times in the mainline for three scenarios.
nodes_process.description: Travel times in the mainline are evaluated for the DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control scenarios, including quartiles and mean values.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 10 presents the temporal-spatial distribution of the mean speeds along the mainline.
nodes_process.description: The temporal-spatial distribution of mean speeds along the mainline is evaluated for the DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control scenarios.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 11 presents the Q1, Q2, and Q3 of the queue lengths at the on-ramp in three scenarios.
nodes_process.description: Queue lengths at the on-ramp are evaluated for the DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control scenarios, including quartiles and mean values.

nodes_process.source_quote: The better performance of the proposed DRL method is further revealed when considering traffic flows downstream of the merge area, which is demonstrated in Figure 14.
nodes_process.description: Traffic flows downstream of the merge area are evaluated for the DRL, PI-ALINEA, and no-control scenarios.

nodes_process.source_quote: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of information contained in video data. As shown in Figure 15, the control area is divided into eight subareas.
nodes_process.description: The control area is divided into eight subareas. Information from each subarea is removed from the original data to generate perturbed data for evaluating the impact of missing information.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 16 presents the box plot of travel time when the information of different subareas is removed, and the baseline is the result of experiments that take original data as input.
nodes_process.description: Travel times are evaluated using perturbed data (with information removed from different subareas) to assess the impact of missing video data information.
